newsitem.title: USA: US High Court clarifies bank false statement law.
newsitem.headline: US High Court clarifies bank false statement law.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court, by an 8-1 vote, sided with the U.S. Justice Department and made it easier for prosecutors to win cases involving false statements by individuals to federally insured banks.

The high court, in an opinion by Justice David Souter, ruled that the importance of the falsehood was not an element of the crime of knowingly making a false statement to the bank under one section of the law.
The justices overturned a ruling by a U.S. appeals court that the importance of the false statement was an issue to be decided by the jury rather than the judge.

The case involved two men, owners and officers of a firm that leased and serviced copier equipment, who were charged in 1993 by prosecutors in Missouri with making false statements to several banks to obtain financing. They also were charged with giving a bank forgeries of their wives' signatures.
They were convicted, but the appeals court threw out the convictions and ordered a new trial.

In the ruling, Souter said the appeals court was wrong. He said Congress in adopting the law at issue did not appear to intend that the importance or "materiality" of the false statement be an element of the crime.
Justice John Paul Stevens was the lone dissenter, noting the law carries a maximum punishment of 30 years in prison and a $1 million fine.
"I am convinced that Congress did not intend this draconian statute to apply to immaterial falsehoods, even when made for the purpose of currying favor with a bank's loan officer," he said.
